title: The agent has an owner. Does its schedule?
summary: A trigger can keep acting after its original decision-maker leaves. Record who approved unattended runs, why they exist, and when they must be reviewed.

sections.title: A run record answers only part of the question
sections.text: A system may record a trigger, an action, and each run. Those records help reconstruct activity. They do not necessarily identify who approved the recurring run, the business purpose it serves, or when the organization should reconsider it.

sections.title: Treat the trigger as part of the authority
sections.text: Add unattended schedules and event triggers to the authorization record. Name the person accountable for the runs, state the business reason, define the permitted effect, and set a review date or change condition.

sections.title: Connect offboarding to active triggers
sections.text: When an owner leaves or changes role, identify the schedules and event triggers they approved. Suspend a trigger until a new accountable owner reviews and accepts it. A reassigned agent does not by itself show that the new owner approved every recurring action.

title: Authorize the chain, not just its parts.
summary: Individual agent permissions do not describe what an orchestration may decide or change as a whole. Define the combined scope and trace each delegation.

sections.title: The outcome belongs to the composition
sections.text: In an orchestration, one agent may retrieve information, another may decide what to do, and a later agent may change a record or contact someone. Reviewing each component separately can leave the combined outcome outside any one agent’s approved scope.

sections.title: Record the chain's authority
sections.text: Identify who initiated the workflow and for what purpose, who approved the composition, which agents act at each delegation step, and what external changes the chain may produce. Name the accountable owner for the combined outcome.

sections.title: Test the handoffs and the final effect
sections.text: Verify that each handoff carries only the authority needed for the next step. Test denied tools, changed inputs, missing agents, and actions outside the chain’s approved effect. Retain evidence for the full sequence, not only the final agent call.

title: Authorization comes before autonomy.
summary: Map agent identity, delegated or application permissions, tool access, denied-action tests, and the process for removing access.

sections.title: Start with the action, not the model
sections.text: A capable model does not establish permission to act. List the resources an agent needs, the actions it can take, and the conditions under which those actions are allowed. Reading a document, changing a record, and sending a message are different permissions.

sections.title: Make the authority traceable
sections.text: Record the business owner, technical maintainer, identity, permitted tools, and approval gates. Distinguish actions taken with a user’s delegated authority from those taken with an application or agent identity. The distinction affects access decisions and evidence.

sections.title: Test the boundary
sections.text: Verify allowed actions and denied actions. Include revoked access, unavailable tools, unexpected input, and actions requiring review. A successful demonstration should not be the only test of an agent.

sections.title: Plan for ownership to change
sections.text: Decide how often to review access and when to remove it. When a sponsor leaves or the workflow changes, someone must decide whether the agent still needs its permissions. The rules for acting independently must be able to change.

title: Modernization is also an AI control.
summary: How an API can enforce approved operations, preserve application rules, and handle failures when AI reaches a legacy system.

sections.title: A connection is not an integration design
sections.text: Connecting a model to a database may make a prototype possible. It does not establish which records may be read, which operations are safe, or how failures should be handled. The application’s operating rules still matter.

sections.title: Expose a deliberate interface
sections.text: An API, an interface for exchanging information between systems, can define approved actions, check incoming information and permissions, and record what happened. Improving an older application can begin with one workflow and its connection to AI.

sections.title: Preserve the business rules
sections.text: Review validation, approval, exception handling, and transaction boundaries before introducing agent access. Rules embedded in an older screen or manual process may not exist at the database layer.

sections.title: Migrate in a controlled scope
sections.text: Define the workflow, allowed actions, verification scenarios, and recovery process. Separate AI-assisted software development from AI-enabled functionality: using a coding assistant does not mean the resulting system contains an agent.

title: Governance that survives deployment.
summary: Connect each AI policy requirement to the system setting, operating procedure, owner, and record that put it into effect.

sections.title: Turn each policy requirement into a system setting or procedure
sections.text: For each requirement, name the system, setting, process, and owner that put it into practice. A rule about information access should identify where permissions are enforced. A rule about approval should name the decision and the person responsible.

sections.title: Separate configuration from operation
sections.text: A configured control needs an operating process. Access reviews, incident response, ownership transfers, and retirement depend on people and records as well as technical settings.

sections.title: Collect useful evidence
sections.text: Choose records that explain what happened, what authority was used, and which control applied. Define retention and access responsibilities. More logs do not automatically provide more accountability.

sections.title: Review when the system changes
sections.text: New tools, data sources, models, and business purposes can change the risk of an existing agent. Make material capability changes a trigger for review rather than waiting for a calendar date.
